source: Wang, Jain, Zhang, Ray, Kumar, Athiwaratkun (2024) Reasoning in Token Economies: Budget-Aware Evaluation of LLM Reasoning Strategies
finding: When compute is matched, chain-of-thought self-consistency (SC) often beats multi-agent debate (MAD), Reflexion and other strategies. SC scores rise smoothly with budget. MAD plateaus and can fall as budget grows. Answer entropy shrinks each debate round, so agents tunnel on one answer.
numbers: MAD with 6 agents overlaps SC exactly up to 6 queries (same strategy). Extra models (GPT-3.5-Turbo-0125, Mistral-7B, LLaMA-2-70b, Mixtral-8x7B) show the same trend. Entropy of debate answers declines round by round (Figure 6).
quote: certain strategies such as multi-agent debate or Reflexion can become worse if more compute budget is utilized
limits: Older models (2024); math and QA benchmarks; LLaMA-2-70b could not run MAD to equal budget because of the 4k context.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: debate is not a free gain at equal tokens. Any debate operator in our scaffold needs an SC arm at the same token count.

source: Tran and Kiela (2026) Single-Agent LLMs Outperform Multi-Agent Systems on Multi-Hop Reasoning Under Equal Thinking Token Budgets
finding: At equal thinking-token budgets, single agents (SAS) match or beat five multi-agent designs (sequential, subtask-parallel, parallel roles, debate, ensemble) on FRAMES and MuSiQue with Qwen3-30B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-70B and Gemini 2.5. Debate is the strongest multi-agent variant. The authors also find budget-control artifacts in the Gemini API that inflate apparent multi-agent gains.
numbers: Table 1 average over models: at 100 thinking tokens SAS .427, sequential .386, subtask .396, roles .417, debate .420, ensemble .411; at 500 tokens SAS .426, debate .420, roles .423. Qwen3-30B FRAMES 500 tokens: SAS .240, debate .206. Gemini 2.5 Flash FRAMES 100 tokens: SAS .333, debate .445 (authors trace such gaps to under-used thinking).
limits: Multi-hop QA only; bootstrap CIs overlap in many cells; theory predicts multi-agent helps when single-agent context use is degraded or compute is large.
agent_relevance: Debate gains vanish when tokens are matched. Same warning as the c literature: do not credit a group structure without a matched control.

source: Hu, Shen, Lakshmipathi (2026) Statistical Scouting Finds Debate-Safe but Not Debate-Useful Cases: A Matched-Ceiling Study
finding: Under a 960-token ceiling, greedy, three-sample voting and two-agent critique-revise debate each win in a different (model, dataset) cell; debate leads only for Llama on MuSiQue. An oracle picking the best protocol per item gains +14.0 and +13.7 points over the best fixed protocol, but cheap vote-entropy routing recovers only 11 to 19% of that gap.
numbers: Vote-entropy threshold: +1.3 pp (Llama), +1.7 pp (Ministral); Fisher combined p=0.22; pooled +1.6 pp, p=0.125. 66% of debate-helpful items occur when voting is unanimous but wrong. Debate uses more of the ceiling than vote3 on MuSiQue, so the match is on ceiling, not actual tokens.
limits: Two 8B open-weight models; MuSiQue and GSM8K; ceiling not actual spend; authors admit a prompt-compliance artifact in their self-critique probe.
agent_relevance: Debate helps on specific items but is hard to route to. Do not make debate a default operator without a measured gate.

source: Bertalanic and Fortuna (2026) The Cost of Consensus: Isolated Self-Correction Prevails Over Unguided Homogeneous Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Teams of 10 homogeneous 7-8B agents (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Ministral-3-8B) debating up to 3 rounds on GSM-Hard and MMLU-Hard fail in three ways: sycophantic conformity, contextual fragility and consensus collapse. Debate costs more for equal or lower accuracy than isolated self-correction.
numbers: Modal adoption up to 85.5%; vulnerability rate (correct answer destabilised) up to 70.0%; oracle gap up to 32.3 pp (correct answer in the pool but plurality discards it); debate uses 2.1 to 3.4 times more tokens, up to 28,631 per problem; conformity is high already at 2 peers.
limits: Small open models, homogeneous teams without roles; does not claim to hold for heterogeneous or structured debate.
agent_relevance: A named failure list for any group operator: conformity, fragility, collapse.

source: Wunderlich, Kaesberg, Wahle, Ruas, Gipp (2026) Multi-Agent Reasoning Improves Compute Efficiency: Pareto-Optimal Test-Time Scaling (ACL SRW)
finding: A counter-result. Across 34 configurations and over 100 evaluations on MMLU-Pro and BBH, at equal compute debate beats self-consistency by 1.3 points and mixture-of-agents by 2.7 points. SC saturates earlier; multi-agent gains persist, mostly on harder items.
numbers: Up to +7.1 points over CoT at 20 times CoT compute on MMLU-Pro. Gain over CoT at 15 to 20 times compute: easy +2.2%, medium +8.5%, hard +9.0%. Design rule: scale agents not rounds for debate; MoA best with one more proposer than layers.
limits: Compute counted in FLOPs; margins of 1.3 to 2.7 points are small; no seed-level CIs seen in the text read.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays mixed: debate or MoA can win at equal FLOPs on hard knowledge items, narrowly. Gate by difficulty and measure.

source: Li, Naito, Shirado (2025/2026) Systematic Failures in Collective Reasoning under Distributed Information in Multi-Agent LLMs (HiddenBench v3, ICML 2026): isolating the bottleneck
finding: Ablations on GPT-4.1 point to surfacing private facts, not reasoning, as the bottleneck. Forcing every agent to disclose all facts in round one lifts post-discussion accuracy from 0.233 to 0.967. A secretary agent that only summarises gives 0.100. One adversarial agent raises accuracy to 0.492, more dissent lowers it.
numbers: Table 6: baseline 0.233, Reveal-All 0.967 (+/-0.033), Secretary 0.100. Table 5: 0 adversarial 0.233; 1 adversarial + 3 default 0.492; 2+2 0.342; 3+1 0.242; 4 adversarial 0.375. Headline over 15 LLMs: 30.1% multi-agent with distributed information vs 80.7% single agent with full information; 65 tasks.
limits: Ablations use GPT-4.1 on three tasks, about 10 sessions per cell; Reveal-All hands over facts for free, so it is an oracle, not a deployable scaffold; token cost per arm not reported. Full-profile accuracy on these 3 tasks was 0.733, so 0.967 above it is as printed.
agent_relevance: Closes much of gap 8: a step that makes each sub-agent state its private facts early hits the exact failure. A passive summariser does not.

source: Li, Naito, Shirado (2026) HiddenBench v3: prompting, depth and group-size ablations
finding: No prompt style closes the hidden-profile gap. Telling agents the information is asymmetric gives 0.367; telling them to share all information gives 0.467. More rounds help up to 15, then hurt. Larger groups gain less from talking.
numbers: Table 3 (average rule): cooperative .200 to .242, conflictual .017, very conflictual .258 (majority 0.000), zero-shot CoT .222, informing asymmetry .367, share all info .467. Table 2: 5 rounds .108, 10 .200, 15 .233, 20 .133. Table 4: improvement from talking +.348 at N=3 (7 tasks), +.250 at N=4 (58 tasks), +.006 at N=7 (5 tasks).
limits: GPT-4.1; N>4 tasks regenerated, so group size is partly confounded with task.
agent_relevance: Group size and rounds are not free levers. Fits Riedl's OR .92 per extra agent.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) Identifying Collective Intelligence Factor in LLM Agent Groups, method details (ACL Findings, pp. 12827-12842)
finding: Re-read for gaps 2 and 10. The group factor is built from group scores on five tasks, all groups run in the one Du et al. debate framework. Individual-agent g per LLM is computed with the same factor method, but the paper text read shows no separate factor analysis of single-model scores compared with the group factor. No repeated runs, seeds or error bars appear in the text read; temperature is 1.0.
numbers: 108 groups: sizes {3,5,8}, rounds {2,3}, 3 topologies, homogeneous or heterogeneous LLMs; tasks commonsense, math, games, coding, writing. Effort = rounds x number of edges (a design setting). Leave-one-task-out correlation of ACI with the held-out task above 0.8 on three tasks and about 0.5 on the other two (p<0.001). Predicted-ACI correlation above 0.6 on commonsense, math, coding, and above an average-performance baseline.
limits: Only 8 LLMs supply member ability, so the factor can mostly track which model is used. Skill congruence is a correlation of g with node degree.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open: the control (single-agent factor vs group factor on same tasks) is not in the paper. Gap 10: no noise estimate found.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) ACI plug-in results, Table 1
finding: Adding predicted ACI to GPTSwarm and G-Designer raised unseen-task scores in all 10 cells reported, but absolute gains are small and each is one run.
numbers: GPTSwarm: commonsense .75 to .77 (+2.7%), math .81 to .91 (+12.3%), game .50 to .53 (+6.0%), coding .87 to .89 (+2.3%), writing .88 to .89 (+1.1%). G-Designer: stated gains 5.5, 3.5, 7.8, 2.4, 2.3%; the extracted table rows for G-Designer are mislabelled, so only the percentages are trusted.
limits: No seeds or CIs; no token-cost comparison; extracted G-Designer rows internally inconsistent.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: gains cannot be separated from run noise on this evidence. Do not copy the plug-in.

source: Crede and Howardson (2017) The structure of group task performance: a second look at collective intelligence (J Applied Psychology 102:1483-1492), via press account
finding: Six published samples reanalysed. Press account: task scores are largely unrelated across areas. Two possible artifacts: low-effort or confused responding (the brick-uses task scored one point per use, some teams scored zero) and nesting, where individual answers averaged into a team score can inflate small covariation. Only Engel 2014 is said to have concluded there was no evidence of c.
numbers: Per-sample first-factor values not obtainable. Crossref confirms the paper (DOI 10.1037/apl0000176) with no abstract.
limits: Press page only; the paywalled full text could not be opened. Gap 3 first-factor values stay open.
agent_relevance: Check agent task batteries for floor effects, such as agents that return nothing on some tasks.

source: Woolley, Kim, Malone (2018) Measuring Collective Intelligence in Groups: A Reply to Credé and Howardson
finding: Search-result summary only (the SSRN page gave 403): the authors accept that measures can improve and that boundaries and mechanisms are open, but say Credé and Howardson do not show enough evidence that the factor does not exist.
limits: Not opened. Do not cite beyond this summary.
agent_relevance: The dispute is partly about measurement and not a clean refutation.

source: Graf, Gimpel, Barlow (2019) Clarifying the Structure of Collective Intelligence in Teams: A Meta-Analysis
finding: Pooled five task-type correlations from 13 studies in 6 papers, 745 teams. A one-factor CFA fits badly and parallel analysis points to three factors. A stricter reading than Rowe 2021.
numbers: Pooled task-type correlations -0.17 to +0.17; average inter-item r=0.001. One-factor CFA chi2=40.79, df=5, CFI .73, TLI .45, RMSEA .10. PAF first eigenvalue 1.05 (threshold 1.38), 17% of variance; second factor 15%. Includes Woolley 2010 (40 and 107 teams), Engel 2014 and 2015, Barlow and Dennis 2016, Bates and Gupta 2017.
limits: Work-in-progress report; only 5 of 8 McGrath task types; pools matrices over face-to-face and online contexts with one moderator.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 (human side): the one-factor model is a choice. Fit one- and two-factor models to agent task scores first.

source: Kommol, Riedl, Woolley (2025) The Structure of Collective Intelligence: Evidence for Collective Memory, Attention, and Reasoning (OSF preprint)
finding: A Woolley-network meta-analysis of 22 studies finds a hierarchical three-factor model (memory, attention, reasoning) fits better than other models, especially in established groups. Even this lab now describes sub-structure under a general factor.
numbers: 22 studies, 5,279 individuals in 1,356 groups (a press release says 5,349 individuals). Fit indices and variance shares not on the page read.
limits: Abstract only. Gap 7 stays open: no AVE or CFI numbers could be read.
agent_relevance: If c has sub-structure, test memory-like, attention-like and reasoning-like skills of the agent separately.

source: Rowe, Hattie, Munro (2024) High-performing teams: Is collective intelligence the answer? (PLOS ONE 19(8): e0307945)
finding: With 85 university students on complex cognitive tasks in individual, group and predictive phases, a two-factor model (crystallised and fluid) fits better than a single factor. Individual and collective measures correlate moderately with later group assignment scores.
numbers: N=85; rs=.40 to .47 for predictive validity of group assignment scores.
limits: Abstract only (cut off in places); small sample; one lab.
agent_relevance: Same message as d12 and d13: a single factor is a modelling choice.

source: Woolley, Chow, Mayo, Riedl, Chang (2022) Collective Attention and Collective Intelligence: The Role of Hierarchy and Team Gender Composition (Organization Science)
finding: A randomised structural manipulation: 146 teams of four were randomly assigned to stable, unstable or unspecified hierarchy. It changed speaking patterns (stable gave cooperative synchronous speech; unstable or none gave more interruptions). CI was a modelled outcome with a gender-by-speech interaction, not a direct treatment effect.
numbers: 584 individuals in 146 teams (4 teams dropped). Direct effect of interactional synchrony on CI B=0.09, p=0.249 (not significant). Majority-female teams higher CI with synchronous speech; all-male teams higher CI with competitive interruptions.
limits: Gap 5: a structural intervention, not a trained rise in c; no held-out task transfer. Same lab network as the original c work.
agent_relevance: Process effects on c depend on composition. No universal debate-order rule follows.

source: McDonald, Nguyen, Botelho, Dishop, Woolley, Gonzalez (2026) Exploring the Effects of Real-Time Feedback on Collaborative Processes to Enhance Collective Intelligence in Teams (Collective Intelligence)
finding: Two randomised experiments with teams of four on an online search-and-rescue task. Live feedback on effort, skill use and coordination changed behaviour but did not raise performance. Effort-only feedback made performance worse because teams neglected coordination.
numbers: Sample sizes and statistics not given on the page read.
limits: Press summary only; full paper not opened; one task type.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: direct attempts to raise a collaboration metric failed or backfired. Optimising a measured process metric is risky, like optimising a c-like score.

source: Gupta, Kim, Glikson, Woolley (2024) Using digital nudges to enhance collective intelligence in online collaboration (MIS Quarterly), search summary
finding: Search summary only: 168 online groups randomly assigned to nudges on skill use, strategy or effort. A nudge to discuss skills and how to apply them raised CI; some other nudges lowered it.
numbers: 168 groups (from the search summary); no effect sizes obtained.
limits: Not opened (the fetch returned the McDonald 2026 release instead). Transfer to held-out tasks not seen.
agent_relevance: Weak support that a skill-discussion step can raise a group score; sign differs by nudge, so test each step.

source: AEA RCT registry 2896 (Deming and Weidmann design) Understanding Collective Intelligence, via search summary
finding: Registry entry: individuals randomised to groups to test whether some people reliably raise team performance and whether this carries to a new problem-solving task. Results not obtained.
numbers: Registry only; outcomes include memory, numerical reasoning and spatial reasoning tasks.
limits: Not opened; no results found, so it closes neither gap 5 nor 9.
agent_relevance: Listed so the gap stays marked open.

source: Search for independent replications of the LLM collective-intelligence factor (Zhou 2026), Nov 2026
finding: No independent replication of the ACI factor was returned. Near hits: Riedl arXiv 2510.05174v3 (information-theoretic test of integrated vs aggregated agents) and a group-size paper (Flint et al., PNAS 2026, per search summary).
limits: Absence in a few searches is weak evidence of absence.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays open for protocols other than debate.
